https://www.dw.com/en/niger-s-failed-cou.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JgEo Following the attempted coup, military units have moved into key positions across the capital, Niamey Image: REUTERS Advertisement What does it mean to be a soldier in Niger today? It means fighting jihadi groups under difficult conditions and at considerable personal risk for little pay, said Sahel expert Abdoulaye Sounaye, a professor at the Leibniz-Zentrum Moderner Orient research institution in Berlin. In an exclusive interview with DW, he described the hard conditions facing Nigerien soldiers: "The vast majority earn less than €150 [about $170] a month, and many have to support six, seven or more family members on that monthly salary." "This naturally contributes to discontent within Niger's armed forces," he added, hinting at some of the motivation behind the increasing levels of discontent among soldiers. At the same time, military personnel are expected to follow a strict military leadership which only came to power through a coup. Junta vs. Islamists At the top of this junta sits General Abdourahamane Tchiani, the commander of the presidential guard prior to the military takeover in 2023. Tchiani ousted democratically elected President Mohamed Bazoum. His junta largely justified its rule by invoking the ongoing fight against jihadi violence in the country, which it claims the Bazoum administration had failed to sufficiently address. But the failed uprising in Niamey over the weekend puts that claim to the test amid growing frustration within the military over the unending battle against Islamist insurgencies. On the weekend, parts of the army temporarily took control of Air Base 101 at Niamey's international airport, and attempted to advance toward the presidential palace and Niger's state broadcaster. From left to right: Mali's Assimi Goita, Niger's Abdourahamane Tchiani and Burkina Faso's Ibrahim Traore posed for photographs during the first ordinary summit of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) in Niamey, Niger, in July 2024 Image: Mahamadou Hamidou/REUTERS The government has described the incident as a mutiny . But Senegalese governance expert Pape Ibrahima Kane told DW that "this was not just a mutiny, but an attempted coup. If this is not an attempted coup, then what does an attempted coup look like?" Growing frustration within the army Niger's military has been fighting jihadi groups for years without managing to contain the violence . The capital, Niamey, has come under attack several times this year alone. For soldiers, this means that they're exposed to high risks daily, compounded by serious problems with equipment, supplies and logistics. Kane described an army struggling to move its troops and equipment across the country's vast territory. Whether the government has the financial resources to address these shortcomings, meanwhile, remains an open question. One soldiers told DW on the strict condition of anonymity that the insurgents they face in battle are often better equipped and quicker to react: "What we really regret is the lack of supplies and equipment. The terrorists are on motorcycles, and we’re in 4x4 vehicles. Three vehicles against twenty or a hundred motorcycles — you can see how complicated it is. Even though our superiors often tell us they’ve ordered the right equipment, we’re still suffering." The soldier went on to say that when they are sent out on a mission, "we always tell ourselves, 'maybe this is the last one.' But what can we do? We have no choice . We are doing it for our country." What's driving Russia's ambitious push into Africa? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video There also appears to be growing frustration over military pay and work conditions. Sahel expert Mamadou Mouth Bane sees the possible preferential treatment of the presidential guard over front-line units as one factor behind the discontent that resulted in the uprising. "The men who are at the front are being neglected. They feel forgotten and treated worse" than the presidential units, Bane explained, highlighting that the junta cannot afford to alienate these soldiers. The military uprising also highlights the junta's chief dilemma: The loyalty of its forces remain key to the current military rulers' ongoing grip on power, which in the light of the latest developments might just be slipping. Russia: Niger's security guarantor The role of Russia's Africa Corps is also particularly significant in this context. The force has taken over large parts of the former activities of Wagner mercenaries in Africa. Following the failed mutiny against the Kremlin of Wagner Group chief Yevgeny Prigozhin and his mysterious death in a plane crash in August 2023, Russia quickly reorganized its operations in Africa, placing them more firmly under the control of its Defense Ministry. In Niger, the Africa Corps has become an important security partner of the junta. During the latest uprising, Russian forces actively helped retake Air Base 101, according to a statement by Russia's ambassador — at the direct behest of the country's military rulers. Russia has engaged in under-the-radar military operations in several countries in Africa Image: French Army/AP/picture alliance By helping the Nigerien army put down an attack from within its own ranks, it is becoming evident that the role of the Africa Corps now reaches well beyond its stated objective of assisting with the military government's counterterrorism strategy. Kane described Niger's reliance on the Africa Corps as a "strategic dependency" in his interview with DW, claiming that the junta would have fallen without Russian assistance. "Without the Russian army, we would have a new government in Niger today," he stressed. Is Tchiani playing Russian roulette? But there are further factors to take into consideration, which could challenge Kane's statement. According to DW information gathered on the ground, the presidential guard and other forces loyal to the regime were also heavily involved in the response to the coup attempt. Algeria — Niger's neighbor to the northwest — meanwhile also backed Niamey, deploying four Su-30 fighter jets to Niger. The involvement of the Africa Corps was probably a decisive factor in the rapid suppression of the uprising, but not the only one. But it appears to have exposed Tchiani's dependence on a foreign armed partner to ensure his grip on power. Fighting jihadi groups under difficult conditions: Soldiers stand guard during a military ceremony at the Martyr Quarter in Niamey Image: Ludovic Marin/AFP A risk for the Sahel at large It's evident that the Africa Corps alone cannot defeat the ongoing insurgency of jihadi groups; otherwise it would have solved the crisis by now after years of involvement in the region. Neither can it solve the Nigerien army's structural problems. This makes Niger a test case for the strength of this security model pursued by the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) , which is comprised of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso. All three military juntas have increasingly been turning to Russia while distancing themselves from Western partners. But Russian support can only help stabilize the juntas in the short term. As long as foreign forces have to take over critical security tasks, the underlying causes of the military crisis remain unresolved. The failed coup attempt was ultimately a victory for Tchiani's junta — but equally a warning sign about the state of Niger's armed forces. In the face of mounting challenges, their loyalty to the regime can clearly no longer be taken for granted. Can new AES Unified Force stamp out terror in the Sahel? https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/world-news.text: An international airport was closed in the capital of Lithuania after what was believed to be a drone sighting - but the actual cause was much less serious. NATO fighter jets were scrambled in Vilnius, Lithuania , as residents received text message alerts. All flights from Vilnius International Airport were suspended during the operation on Sunday. The yellow alert, issued by LT72 - Lithuania's emergency platform - was sent out at around 1pm local time (11am BST). It read: "AIR RAID ALERT (YELLOW). Potentially detected drone. Find a safe place. If you see a suspicious object, keep away, call 112. Wait for the all-clear." The alert was sent out to those in Vilnius city, Elektrėnai district, Trakai district and Vilnius district. It was in place for just under 40 minutes. Flights at Vilnius International Airport have now resumed. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the National Crisis Management Center, told LRT radio: "People can calm down. (...) In principle, the threat level has been eliminated." After the situation was dealt with, residents in Vilnius received an alert stating: "The Lithuanian Armed Forces inform: air alert is over. You may leave safe places or shelters." This morning, the Lithuanian military said that Air Force radars near Varena had detected a target, thought to be a drone, moving in the direction of Kaliningrad and had likely entered Lithuania from Belarus . The military later said: "After the radar tag left Lithuanian airspace, there was no reason to declare an air alert." But it has now been determined that the unidentified object was actually a flock of birds, 15min reports . The National Crisis Management Center stated: "Fighter jets carrying out a NATO air policing mission were deployed to inspect the object. "They determined that the radar signals were a flock of birds. In the initial radar information, the markings of birds and drones may be similar, therefore, an additional check was carried out to accurately determine the nature of the object."

Screen capture/cbf.net/podgaisky Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save For 20 years, Mina Podgaisky and her husband, Gennady, ministered to street children in Ukraine. Then Russia’s invasion forced them out, and their mission moved across the border to Poland. The couple, both pastors and counselors, began their work in Kyiv in 2002 as field personnel for the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship, which provides global outreach and ministry services. Mina Podgaisky is originally from Chihuahua, Mexico, and Gennady Podgaisky is from Russia. “We felt a call from the Lord to go and serve the street children of Ukraine,” Podgaisky said. “At that time, there were between 17,000 and 24,000 street children. So the country had a major crisis.” Podgaisky spoke about the couple’s ministry to members of First Baptist Church in Elizabeth City, a CBF member church, at a dinner in August. After starting in Kyiv, the capital, the Podgaiskys established the Village of Hope Ministry Center in Bucha, northwest of the city. The center was built on the site of a former Soviet Pioneer camp, where young people spent summers in state-sponsored ideological training, or, as Podgaisky put it, “where they sent the children to introduce them to Communism.” The couple rented about 9 acres of forest land from the Ukrainian government for $500 a year and bought the existing buildings, Podgaisky said. They also built new housing for foster families, children and orphans. At one point, the village was home to two foster families and 24 children. The Podgaiskys were in the United States when Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, and they hoped the war would end quickly. When the fighting began, bombs and other sounds of war could be heard from the village. In May 2022, the couple began looking for a new ministry location. They still hoped to return to Ukraine until Russia began bombing hospitals, Podgaisky said. After a children’s hospital in Kyiv was struck, the company that insured their ministry told them it could no longer cover them in Ukraine, citing an “active war that does not discriminate between a hospital and a school for children.” After praying about where to go next, the couple settled on Krakow, in southern Poland, as the nearest suitable location. “We have been there two years,” Podgaisky said. “We still feel the call to serve Ukrainians.” In Krakow, the couple assist Ukrainian refugees whose “hearts are broken” because of the war. “You understand that?” she asked the audience. “Every single Ukrainian, it doesn’t matter where they are in the world, their hearts are broken.” Every week for a year, the couple hosted displaced Ukrainians, Podgaisky said. “One time we had a couple that came in and they spent 17 hours speaking to us.” The families often talk about the trauma they are living through. “They just talk and talk and talk” because they have kept their experiences to themselves, she said. “You can’t share that story with your neighbors, because they’ve already experienced that.” Many have no one to help them “release” the grief they have kept bottled up, she said. “So, we just hold space, is how we call it, for all their grief,” Podgaisky said. “We cry with them, we pray with them and then we say, ‘You sleep as long as you can.’” To learn more about the Podgaiskys’ ministry or to donate, visit their Facebook page at facebook.com/Podgaiskys or pro.gofundme.com/campaign/gennady-and-mina-podgaisky-2/c584603 . The Cooperative Baptist Fellowship is online at cbf.net .
